name: Teff and finger millet farming in the northern Ethiopian highlands
summary: In the northern Ethiopian and Eritrean highlands, probable domesticated grains of teff, a local cereal, appear about 400 BCE; finger millet is first recorded about 50 BCE to 150 CE.
description: Three probable domesticated teff grains, two from Mezber in Tigray and one from Mai Chiot near Asmara, date to about 400 BCE and are the earliest macrobotanical evidence of the crop; finger millet is first recorded at Bieta Giyorgis in the Early Aksumite period, about 50 BCE to 150 CE. Starch and phytoliths on grinding stones show that people at Mezber had been using C4 grains, probably wild, since about 1600 BCE, alongside barley introduced from outside the highlands. The study leaves open when these cereals were domesticated and says nothing datable about ensete.

impact.note: Teff became a staple of one region, the Ethiopian and Eritrean highlands (reach 1), adding a new native cereal to a farming system that already had introduced barley (depth 2), with few known successors elsewhere (generativity 1).

date.label: c. 400 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Teff first appears in the macrobotanical record about 400 BCE, at Mezber in Tigray and at Mai Chiot near Asmara.

evidence.supports: T’ef is considered to have been domesticated locally, but it does not appear in the macrobotanical record until ca. 400 BCE at Mezber (Tigrai, Ethiopia) and Mai Chiot (Asmara, Eritrea)

date.label: c. 50 BCE to 150 CE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Finger millet is first recorded at Bieta Giyorgis in Tigray in the Early Aksumite period, about 50 BCE to 150 CE.

evidence.supports: finger millet is recorded for the first time at Bieta Giyorgis (Tigrai, Ethiopia) during the Early Aksumite period (ca. 50 BCE to 150 CE)

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The teff evidence is three probable domesticated grains; the paper's own microbotanical results suggest domesticated C4 forms were taken up only around or after the start of the Common Era, so the date of domestication is open.
Whether any native crop was cultivated before barley arrived is unsettled; the paper reports C4 grain use, probably wild, at Mezber from about 1600 BCE.
Ensete, noog and coffee from the lead have no dated evidence here.
Mezber is placed by its district, Gulo Makeda, with approximate coordinates; Bieta Giyorgis is placed at the hill beside Aksum from the supervisor's own knowledge, not from the paper.

research.note: The paper says teff is considered to have been domesticated locally but that the origin and time of domestication of the Horn's C4 cereals remain unknown, and that barley from outside was already grown there by about 1600 BCE.
